readerTitle: Your best plumber is slipping. What do you do first?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (배관 서비스 회사, 레스토랑 주방) + 실제 연구 1건 (Koval 외, 2015)
insight: 뛰어난 직원이 흔들리면 사람보다 먼저 그에게 쌓인 일을 의심한다. 잘하는 사람일수록 일이 몰리기 때문이다.
misconception: 최고의 직원은 알아서 회복한다. 성과가 떨어졌다면 동기가 떨어졌거나 태도가 변한 것이다.

sources.text: Koval, C. Z., vanDellen, M. R., Fitzsimons, G. M., & Ranby, K. W. (2015). The burden of responsibility: Interpersonal costs of high self-control. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 108(5), 750–766.
시나리오와 인물은 모두 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Koval 외(2015) 연구의 핵심 결과를 다시 확인하세요. 자기통제력이 높은 사람에게 주변 사람들이 더 많은 일을 기대하고 맡기며, 그 일이 그 사람에게 드는 노력을 과소평가한다는 내용입니다. 카드 6에서는 수치 없이 일반적으로만 서술했습니다.
배관 회사, 재방문 건수, 레스토랑 주방은 모두 가상 설정입니다. 재방문 "한 분기 1건 → 이번 달 3건"은 설명용 수치입니다.

cards.title: Your best plumber is slipping. What do you do first?
body: You run a 12-person plumbing company. Maya has been your best technician for six years. Customers ask for her by name.
This month, three of her jobs needed a callback. She usually has one a quarter. She was late twice and short with a customer. You have four decisions to make.

image.label: A skilled plumber looking tired beside a van at dusk
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 해 질 녘, 작업 밴 옆에서 공구 가방을 든 숙련된 여성 배관공이 지친 표정으로 휴대폰 일정을 보고 있음. 일정 화면에 일이 빽빽하게 쌓여 있음. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

options.text: Mention it at the morning crew meeting so everyone tightens up
options.feedback: Everyone knows who you mean. Maya feels called out in public and gets defensive, and the crew learns that slips get aired in front of the team.

options.text: Book 30 private minutes this week to share what you've seen and ask what's going on
options.feedback: You get her side before you form a view, and she hears it from you privately, not through gossip.

options.text: Give it a few weeks. Top performers usually sort themselves out
options.feedback: You avoid an awkward talk, but callbacks keep costing money, and Maya may read your silence as not noticing or not caring.

cards.title: She says she's fine, just busy.
body: Say you chose the private meeting. Maya sits down, arms crossed. "I'm fine. It's just a busy stretch."

options.text: Accept it and say your door is open
options.feedback: Kind, and it keeps things calm. But nothing changes, and next month you have the same talk with more callbacks behind it.

options.text: Name the facts calmly: three callbacks this month. Then ask what's making the job harder, and wait
options.feedback: Specific facts are hard to brush off but don't attack her. The silence gives her room to answer for real.

options.text: Tell her you need the old Maya back
options.feedback: It sounds like praise, but it judges her as a person. She hears that she's failing, and she closes up.

cards.title: Now you hear the real story.
body: Say you named the facts and waited. After a pause, Maya explains. Since spring you gave her two apprentices to train and every tricky job. She does their paperwork at night. Her father is also unwell.

options.text: Give her a bonus for carrying so much
options.feedback: It shows you value her, but money doesn't add hours. She stays just as stretched, now with a reason to feel guilty for slipping.

options.text: Sort her work together: what she keeps, what moves to someone else, what stops
options.feedback: You fix the cause, not the symptom, and she helps shape the plan, so she's more likely to own it.

options.text: Tell her to take a week off
options.feedback: Rest helps, but she returns to the same pile of work. The week ends and the problem is still there.

cards.title: You have a plan. How do you follow up?
body: Say you sorted the work together. One apprentice moves to another tech. The office takes the routine paperwork. Maya keeps the hard jobs she enjoys.

options.text: Trust her and check back if problems return
options.feedback: It shows respect, but you'll only hear about trouble once it's big again.

options.text: A 15-minute check-in each week for a month, watching callbacks together
options.feedback: You both see early whether the plan works and can adjust it before small problems grow.

options.text: Check her job reports every day and message her about each one
options.feedback: You'd spot every problem, but it tells your best person you no longer trust her.

cards.title: When a strong performer slips, look at the load first.
body: Reliable people get more work. Each extra task seems small, and nobody adds them up. That's the trap you walked into with Maya.
Research backs this up. Koval and colleagues (2015) found that people expect more from those with high self-control, and underestimate how much effort that work costs them.
So **diagnose before you judge**. A sudden slip from a proven person is usually a signal about the job, not the person.

image.label: A pile of small tasks stacked on one worker's toolbox
image.brief: 공구 상자 하나 위에 작은 메모지 카드가 탑처럼 쌓여 흔들리는 그림. 카드마다 "Train apprentice", "Tricky job", "Paperwork", "Just one more". 옆 공구 상자들은 비어 있음.

cards.title: In a kitchen, it's the best line cook.
body: A head chef notices her strongest cook plating slower and snapping at servers. The cause: he's been covering every sick call and training each new hire during service.
The same four moves apply. Talk privately, name the facts, sort the load together, and check in weekly.

image.label: A line cook juggling several stations at once
image.brief: 레스토랑 주방. 한 요리사가 그릴, 튀김, 플레이팅 스테이션을 동시에 맡고 있고 다른 직원들이 그에게 질문하는 모습. 실제 상표 없음.

cards.softwareNote: In software, it's the engineer everyone pings. They get pulled into every outage and code review until their own work stalls. Count their interruptions before you question their output.

cards.title: Overload isn't always the answer.
body: Sometimes the cause is something else: a skill gap, a clash with a colleague, or lost interest. Asking first lets you find out.
You don't need private details. "My father is unwell" is enough to plan around.
If the plan is fair and slips continue, it becomes a performance conversation. And make sure moving her work doesn't quietly overload someone else.

cards.title: Ask before you judge, then fix the load together.
body: Each decision used one skill from this unit:
list: **Sorting the work:** delegating and setting expectations
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list everything your most reliable person now does that wasn't in the job six months ago.
